content.title: Artemis II mission set to launch from Kennedy Space Center Wednesday
content.text: Updated March 31, 2026, 3:52 p.m. ETFour astronauts are scheduled to launch on the Artemis II mission for a 10-day trip around the moon.This will be the first time humans have traveled beyond Earth's orbit in over 50 years.The launch is planned for Wednesday, April 1, from Kennedy Space Center in Florida.Local officials are warning residents of major traffic increases due to the historic launch.Four astronauts are set to launch on the Artemis II mission Wednesday, April 1, from Florida, setting off on what will be a 10-day trip around the moon — and the farthest into space since the Apollo missions.The four astronauts, commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, will launch atop the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket in the Orion spacecraft.They will be the first humans in more than 50 years to leave Earth orbit and travel around the moon. Astronauts have not traveled beyond Earth orbit since the 1972 Apollo 17 mission.Where will Artemis II launch from?On launch day, the SLS rocket will liftoff from Kennedy Space Center Pad 39B. The sight is the most northern launch pad at Kennedy Space Center, and has not seen a launch since the 2022 Artemis I mission. It was previously home to space shuttle and Saturn V launches.The rocket has been waiting at the pad since the early hours of March 20. The rocket had rolled out earlier but needed to return to the Vehicle Assembly Buiding for repairs earlier this year.Why is NASA Artemis II flying around the moon?Artemis II will be the first crewed test flight of the SLS rocket and Orion spacecraft. The mission will not land on the moon, but fly around as it tests the spacecraft's capabilities.It will set the stage for the Artemis III mission, which is set to launch in 2027. That mission will take a crew of four to Earth orbit, testing the ability of the Orion spacecraft to dock with one of the lunar landers available for the 2028 Artemis IV landing — either a SpaceX Starship or Blue Origin Mark II.NASA has contracted both SpaceX and Blue Origin to provide lunar landers for the upcoming Artemis missions. Just recently, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman announced the goal of a permanent NASA moon base, locking in on going back to the moon to stay. This is all in preparation for eventually sending humans to Mars.NASA Artemis II launch weatherAs of Monday afternoon, NASA was still on track for a launch attempt beginning at 6:24 p.m. Wednesday, April 1 from Kennedy Space Center Pad 39B. The only watch item NASA has mentioned is weather, which is forecasted to be 80% favorable.As of Tuesday morning, the weather was still forecast to be 80% favorable for the launch attempt. Currently, the main weather concern is a cumulus cloud violation, which may pose a lightning risk.NASA has a two hour window in which the launch can be attempted.When is the Artemis II moon launch?While the launch is currently set for no earlier than 6:24 p.m. Wednesday, April 1, additional available launch times are as follows:7:22 p.m. April 28:00 p.m. April 38:53 p.m. April 49:40 p.m. April 510:36 p.m. April 66:06 p.m. April 30Where to see the Artemis II SLS rocket in Florida?Multiple parks on the Indian River in Titusville provide a view directly across to the Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral launch pads. At the right location, the general public can get an unobstructed glimpse of history sitting on the launch pad.Space View Park, 8 Broad St., TitusvilleRotary Riverfront Park, 4141 S. Washington Ave., TitusvilleKennedy Point Park, 4915 S Washington Ave, Titusville, FL 32780Parrish Park at Titusville, 1 A. Max Brewer Memorial Pkwy, Titusville, FL 32796Artemis II launch traffic in Brevard County, Space CoastBrevard EOC has posted multiple warnings urging county residents to run errands before launch day and expect a major traffic increase, as tourists flock to the Space Coast to witness history.As many as 400,000 people are expected to be on the Space Coast for the launch.Once the Artemis II mission takes off, all traffic returning from the Cape and beaches will flow from east on SR 528 to A1A South and then over to SR 520.Artemis II launch coverageThe FLORIDA TODAY Space Team will provide live updates beginning 10 a.m. on launch day at FloridaToday.com/Space.This will include a running countdown clock, live updates on the progression toward launch, local traffic and local scene updates.Brooke Edwards is a Space Reporter for Florida Today.
